notes.bp: Explain why the second formant bends in an S shape while a speaker moves through vowel-consonant-vowel syllables.
notes.wh: The acoustic trajectory reflects several moving articulators and planning regimes; a purely acoustic curve does not say which physical movement caused it.
notes.naive: Fit a curve to the spectrogram and treat the curve as a direct articulatory law.
notes.ap: Generate the same VCV sequences with an articulatory model, separate vowel transitions from consonant influence, and compare the resulting trajectories and locus equations.
notes.mech: The study uses the Maeda articulatory model to reproduce Öhman's S-shaped F2 trajectories and reassesses conventional locus-equation interpretations.
notes.math: The acoustic pattern is an effect of coordinated movement: a model can test whether the pattern follows from planning constraints rather than treating it as an unexplained spectral shape.
notes.ww: The paper reports synthetic trajectories resembling the observed sequences and structured effects of articulatory planning.
notes.limits: Model geometry, trajectory planning, corpus, and synthetic-to-observed comparison limit claims; matching a trajectory does not identify a unique human motor plan.
notes.title: Articulatory modeling of the S-shaped F2 trajectories observed in Öhman's spectrographic analysis of VCV syllables

notes.bp: A real-time echo canceller may process only 10-ms frames, but each frame still needs enough surrounding context to avoid audible boundary glitches.
notes.wh: Long context can improve continuity but usually adds delay; short-frame training exposes boundaries that long offline examples hide.
notes.naive: Use long frames, add post-processing, or train on isolated short chunks and accept discontinuities.
notes.ap: Keep long-context information in each training batch while producing short-frame outputs, so the model learns continuity without increasing application delay.
notes.mech: The paper proposes Extended Loss for acoustic echo cancellation with short audio frames and limited latency.
notes.math: The loss supervises the local output using context that spans frame boundaries; training context and inference delay are separated rather than traded as the same quantity.
notes.ww: The paper reports reduced boundary discontinuities and improved short-frame AEC performance under the tested real-time conditions.
notes.limits: Echo paths, frame size, batch context, hardware, and evaluation signals bound the claim; continuity on the benchmark is not proof of every room or device.
notes.title: Extended Loss: Incorporating Long Context into Training Models when using Short Audio Frames

notes.bp: Speech models may represent concepts differently from text models, and a joint model may combine or distort those structures rather than simply inheriting text knowledge.
notes.wh: Latent concepts are not directly labeled; comparing modalities requires a method that exposes structure without pretending an interpretation is a measured neuron-level fact.
notes.naive: Inspect nearest words or report downstream accuracy and call the result a theory of concept formation.
notes.ap: Use latent concept analysis to compare speech-only, text-only, and joint foundation models and ask which conceptual structures are shared or modality-specific.
notes.mech: The paper analyzes concept formation in speech and text-based foundation models using an unsupervised latent-concept method.
notes.math: Concept formation is treated as a representation-comparison problem: the analysis proposes interpretable structure, while cross-modal differences reveal what the training signal makes easy or hard to encode.
notes.ww: The paper reports comparative latent conceptual structures across speech, text, and joint models.
notes.limits: Model choice, layer, analysis method, prompts, and human interpretation bound the claim; a latent cluster is not automatically a human concept.
notes.title: From Words to Waves: Analyzing Concept Formation in Speech and Text-Based Foundation Models

notes.bp: Emotion recognition should generalize when people express the same emotion differently, across audio and other modalities and across related tasks.
notes.wh: Individual expression varies with speaker, gender, context, and modality; a parameter-efficient update can share too little or force unrelated tasks together.
notes.naive: Use one shared LoRA update or train a separate full model for every emotion task.
notes.ap: Combine shared LoRA experts, task-specific experts, a memory mechanism, and gender as an auxiliary task to separate common structure from expression-specific variation.
notes.mech: MMLoRA is a multitask memory parameter-efficient method for multimodal speech emotion recognition.
notes.math: The adaptation has two roles: shared parameters carry reusable affective structure, while expert and memory paths preserve task/person-specific differences instead of overwriting them.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved multimodal SER generalization over the tested parameter-efficient baselines.
notes.limits: Datasets, gender labels, task mix, memory policy, modalities, and expression cultures bound the result; auxiliary gender is not a complete model of individual variation.
notes.title: MMLoRA: Multitask Memory Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Multimodal SER

notes.bp: An audio classifier may need to learn new classes one at a time with only a few examples, without forgetting classes it already knows.
notes.wh: The class vocabulary changes and few examples encourage overfitting; a representation that works for old classes may not expose the right view for new ones.
notes.naive: Fine-tune on each new class and accept forgetting, or keep fixed prototypes and ignore representation drift.
notes.ap: Fuse multiple views of the audio and perturb parameters during few-shot class-incremental learning to improve coverage and reduce overfitting.
notes.mech: The paper proposes multi-view fusion and parameter perturbation for few-shot class-incremental audio classification.
notes.math: Adaptation is a balance between plasticity and retention: multiple views supply evidence while controlled perturbation tests whether a decision is stable rather than memorized.
notes.ww: The paper reports class-incremental classification results against the tested baselines.
notes.limits: Class order, shots, audio domains, perturbation settings, and memory protocol bound the result; benchmark retention does not establish lifelong robustness.
notes.title: Multi-view Fusion and Parameter Perturbation for Few-Shot Class-Incremental Audio Classification

notes.bp: A deepfake detector must learn new attack types while remembering older ones, even when its memory buffer can hold only a small sample of past audio.
notes.wh: Uniform rehearsal misses rare acoustic characteristics and can make the buffer biased toward easy or common examples.
notes.naive: Store random old clips or retrain from scratch whenever a new attack appears.
notes.ap: Generate auxiliary labels describing audio characteristics and use them to sample a more diverse rehearsal memory during continual learning.
notes.mech: RAIS uses auxiliary-informed sampling for rehearsal-based continual audio-deepfake detection.
notes.math: The memory is selected for coverage of acoustic factors, not only class labels; retaining varied evidence helps the detector update without collapsing onto the newest attack.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved continual deepfake detection over rehearsal baselines on new attacks.
notes.limits: Attack families, auxiliary-label quality, buffer size, stream order, and detector threshold bound the result; no finite memory guarantees future attack coverage.
notes.title: Rehearsal with Auxiliary-Informed Sampling for Audio Deepfake Detection

notes.bp: A cinematic separator should keep laughter and screams with the speech stem, because acted nonverbal voice is part of a scene rather than an ordinary sound effect.
notes.wh: Existing datasets often contain read speech, so a model can learn the wrong boundary and remove emotionally heightened vocal sounds as noise or effects.
notes.naive: Train on reading-style stems and assume the separator's speech category matches film dialogue.
notes.ap: Build a dataset whose speech stem includes nonverbal vocalizations and test whether that changes separation behavior on cinematic mixtures.
notes.mech: DnR-nonverbal is a cinematic audio source-separation dataset containing laughter, screams, and other nonverbal sounds in the speech stem.
notes.math: The dataset changes the category definition presented to the model: the target is a vocal event in context, not a narrow phonetic transcript.
notes.ww: The paper reports that conventional separators mishandle nonverbal sounds and that the new dataset improves the tested synthetic separation task.
notes.limits: Synthetic mixtures, labels, scene distribution, separator, and nonverbal taxonomy bound the result; real-film generalization remains open.
notes.title: DnR-nonverbal: Cinematic Audio Source Separation DatasetContaining Non-Verbal Sounds

notes.bp: Haitian Creole needs speech models trained on its own sounds and data, not only a large multilingual model that may underrepresent its structure.
notes.wh: Large multilingual pretraining can help but may encode data imbalance; training a monolingual model from scratch costs data and compute and must be compared fairly.
notes.naive: Fine-tune a multilingual checkpoint and assume scale always beats language-specific training.
notes.ap: Pretrain monolingual self-supervised models for Haitian Creole, compare them with multilingual and French-based models, and fine-tune all for ASR.
notes.mech: The paper develops self-supervised speech-processing models for Haitian Creole and compares monolingual, multilingual, and French-derived initialization.
notes.math: Representation quality depends on language fit as well as parameter count; a smaller language-specific model can win when its pretraining signal matches the target speech.
notes.ww: The paper reports monolingual models that are competitive with or surpass larger multilingual alternatives on the tested ASR tasks.
notes.limits: Data volume, speakers, orthography, model size, pretraining compute, and evaluation domain limit generalization to the broader Creole speech community.
notes.title: Self-Supervised Models of Speech Processing for Haitian Creole
